evidence.text: Look for. • Category selection mechanics: Target existing, massive categories so you do not have to educate the consumer on what the product is. Look for a "sea of sameness" where all incumbents look identical (e.g., all dish soaps are green and toxic; all vitamins are round and pseudo-scientific). • Cultural shift mapping: Identify a macro trend happening elsewhere (e.g., "boutique fitness as a spiritual pursuit") and apply it to the stagnant category (e.g., daily vitamins) to create "creative tension." • Cross-industry theft mechanics: Steal aesthetics from completely unrelated industries. The further apart the dots, the more powerful the idea (e.g., stealing high-end houseware vase shapes and applying them to dish soap packaging). • The "One Iteration" Rule: Change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation. If you change two or three things simultaneously, the product becomes "too novel," breaking consumer adoption. • Naming constraints: The holy grail of brand naming is one word, four letters. Identify a core "jumping-off word" based on the product's ultimate goal (e.g., "technique" for cleaning -> Method; "friendly" for vitamins -> Olly), and base the naming search purely on that feeling.

cards.title: Target existing massive categories to avoid consumer education
cards.claim: Category selection should target existing, massive categories so the consumer does not need to be educated on what the product is.
cards.action: Select a category that already exists at large scale rather than creating a new category that requires educating consumers about the product.
applies_when: choosing which product category to enter
consumer already understands the product type
do_not_use_when: the category is small or the product concept requires consumer education
unknowns: how category size or massiveness is measured
thresholds for deciding a category is massive enough
evidence_quotes: Target existing, massive categories so you do not have to educate the consumer on what the product is.

cards.title: Look for a 'sea of sameness' among incumbents
cards.claim: A category with a 'sea of sameness' is one where all incumbents look identical, such as all dish soaps being green and toxic or all vitamins being round and pseudo-scientific.
cards.action: Identify categories where incumbents appear visually or conceptually identical to locate differentiation opportunity.
applies_when: assessing incumbents in a target category
do_not_use_when: incumbents already differ substantially in appearance or positioning
unknowns: whether sameness guarantees a viable opportunity
evidence_quotes: Look for a "sea of sameness" where all incumbents look identical (e.g., all dish soaps are green and toxic; all vitamins are round and pseudo-scientific).

cards.title: Change only one major variable from the core product expectation
cards.claim: Changing exactly one major variable from the core product expectation supports consumer adoption, while changing two or three simultaneously makes the product 'too novel' and breaks adoption.
cards.action: Limit product changes to exactly one major variable from the core product expectation.
applies_when: designing a product variation from an existing category expectation
do_not_use_when: the intent is to change multiple core product variables at once
unknowns: what counts as a major variable
empirical evidence for the adoption threshold
evidence_quotes: Change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation.
If you change two or three things simultaneously, the product becomes "too novel," breaking consumer adoption.
